disappear.title: Decisions are made, but are they reasoned and communicated systematically?
disappear.intro: Walk through what happens when a significant choice is made. A recommendation is presented. Alternatives are discussed, sometimes cursorily. A direction is chosen; a follow-up goes out. What almost never survives the meeting is the reasoning: the options weighed, the criteria that decided it, the assumptions it rests on, and the owner who committed. The outcome becomes visible. The logic that produced it evaporates.

anatomy.eyebrow: The anatomy of a good decision
anatomy.title: Judge the process, not the outcome.
anatomy.intro: Decision science does not promise the right answer. It promises something more durable: that a rigorous process yields decisions as good as the information allows, and that their quality can be measured, improved, and learned from. Judging a decision by its result alone is a trap behavioral economists call outcome bias.

process.title: Four phases, twelve steps.
process.intro: This is not an abstract checklist. It is a response to failure modes the literature has documented for sixty years. The right analysis in the wrong order produces the wrong decision as reliably as no analysis at all. Weight scales with stakes: a Light decision runs a core subset; Standard and Heavy run all twelve; a Fast-track call is logged on one screen.

tiers.title: Not all decisions deserve the same weight.
tiers.intro: Conflating the three tiers is one of the most common and costly failures in management. Organizations over-govern decisions that should iterate, and under-govern the ones that lock in a decade. The misallocation isn't random. It's behavioral, and it's correctable by design.

bias.title: Bias is not a character flaw. It's a systems problem.
bias.intro: Executives know the vocabulary: anchoring, sunk cost, groupthink. They return from the offsite resolved to decide differently, and nothing changes. Individual awareness does not remove the organizational conditions that activate bias. The response is not behavioral. It is architectural: a record, phase-separation, and a feedback loop. These six earn their place by activating frequently, doing directional damage, and yielding to process design.

ai.title: AI advises. The human decides. Always.
ai.intro: Management decisions are not primarily an analytical problem. They are an organizational commitment problem, and the two require different instruments. AI expands the decision-maker's field of view; it does not carry the moral accountability the choice demands. That accountability requires someone who can be questioned, explain their reasoning, and bear the consequences of being wrong.

principles.title: The rules a practitioner can hold themselves to.
principles.intro: Specific enough to constrain, honest enough to be tested. Adopt them for the next decision on your desk. No platform required.

toolkit.title: Put it to work on your next decision.
toolkit.intro: A pre-decision checklist you can run in five minutes, and a one-page decision record you can print and fill in by hand. Nothing to install.

assessment.title: Where does your organization actually stand?
assessment.intro: Five questions, answered honestly, usually reveal more than a strategy offsite. Answer for how decisions actually get made today, not how the org chart says they should.

platform.title: A decision framework, and the platform to run it.
platform.intro: Arbitara combines a practitioner's decision framework with the technology to operate it — capturing, governing, and learning from every decision, so accountability and speed stop trading against each other.

hero.headline: The power to decide is a discipline, not a talent.
hero.lede: Organizations map their processes, model their architectures, and instrument everything they do. Then they make their most consequential choices in a room, with no structure, no record, and no way to learn from what happens next. Arbitara is a practitioner's field guide to closing that gap.

record.name: The one-page decision record
record.body: A single sheet with every field group (context, governance, options & criteria, assumptions & outcomes) ready to print or fill in a document. It's the smallest possible version of treating a decision as an object.
